text.p: Following are some of the leading stories in the Swedish papers on Wednesday. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.

- Opposition Conservative party leader Carl Bildt said criticism of Prime Minister Goran Persson's remarks on China was exaggerated and had not harmed the country's interests. Bildt said Persson's address to Swedish businessmen in Beijing, where he praised China's political stability, was "embarrassing" but no more than a diplomatic gaffe and Bildt in a newspaper article said Swedish parties should now work towards a joint position on the principles of its China policy.

- World Bank head James Wolfensohn criticised Sweden for failing so far to pledge any financial help to writing off the debt of the world's poorest countries. In a speech in Stockholm, Wolfensohn, who is campaigning to lift the debt burden of the 41 worst affected countries, said only Denmark out of the Nordic countries had so far come up with cash.

- Sweden's indecision over Economic and Monetary Union is affecting its medium to long-term debt rates. For some days now the rate on Sweden's 10-year government bond is higher than for the equivalent maturity in Spain, which is committed to joining EMU from the start. Lenders are demanding a premium in the form of higher rates for countries which may not take part in EMU. "The reason is simple - Spain wants to join while Sweden wants to stay outside," said one dealer in Stockholm.

- Swedish major electricity consumers are banding together to influence prices of the utility. Pharmacia & Upjohn and Aga are among the corporate users joining a new organisation, Elbruk, which introduces itself today. "Previously, when the electricity market was mentioned it was only the producer side that people paid attention to. It's now time for consumers to have their say," said Lars Blomqvist, chairman of Elbruk and in charge of energy purchasing for employment agency Samhall.

- A handful of small companies in Sweden's deregulated post services are challenging the state Post Office, some of them with their own mailboxes, stamps and all with competitively low rates. Any company which fulfills basic criteria and lodges a 20,000 crown deposit with the post and telegraph regulatory body can start delivering mail in Sweden.

- The Post Office is altering the text on its 38,000 mail boxes which at present say letters posted by a certain time will be delivered the next working day. Svenska Dagbladet discovered that one in seven letters was late, and Post officials confronted with the evidence admitted that the text was more of a target than a pledge.

- Finance Minister Erik Asbrink, who has raised the issue of state pension funds investing more in shares, commissioned a report to this effect as early as 1991 when he was deputy finance minister. The report suggested a reorganisation of the so-called AP funds and new rules allowing them to diversify into stocks and overseas investments instead of interest-bearing securities in Sweden.

- Swedish businessmen Fredrik Lundberg is under pressure to take advantage of favourable prices on the Stockholm bourse to sell his holding in building company Siab to Skanska and at the same time become a significant holder of Skanska by snapping up Custos's holding, the paper's bourse commentator said.

- The top 24 listed Swedish companies increased their liquidity from 69.5 billion crowns to 86 billion in the past year, including a 500 percent increase by utility Gullspang, while ceramic goods firm Hoganas increased its cash by 263 percent. Finance directors said the cash would be used to pay off loans, bonuses, high-yield investments or company acquisitions.
